title: The security properties this directory knows how to ask about, and which of them anything actually implements
readMeFirst: This file is a catalogue, not a claim of coverage. Most entries have extractor: null and status: unimplemented, and that is the point: a policy that names a property with no reachable checkpoint has to be exit 3, and a caller can only know that if this file says which properties those are.

status has FOUR values, and this sentence said three until 2026-08-18 while the file below already used the fourth. 'implemented' means an extractor exists and a fixture in this repository measures this property in this configuration. 'candidate' means the extractor exists and would take this configuration, but nothing here has measured it, so nobody should quote it as evidence. 'unimplemented' means there is no extractor at all. 'partial' means an extractor measures part of what the title claims and the entry's statusDetail says which part -- it is used by exactly one entry (notappear.forbidden-external-call), which is how a fourth value stayed unlisted: a reader checking the vocabulary against the catalogue would have to count all 24 entries to notice. Current distribution, recomputed rather than remembered: implemented 7, unimplemented 14, candidate 2, partial 1.

observeAt is per checkpoint, not per property, because a property is very often observable at one checkpoint and not at another, and flattening that into a single list is how a partial check comes to look like a whole one.

ir.wipe-effect.counts: Call sites to a configured effect symbol, resolved from the call instruction with CallBase::getCalledFunction, plus inline stores of a zero constant whose underlying object is an alloca in the unit or a pointer parameter of it. Counted inside one IR function.
ir.wipe-effect.whyBothForms: Above -O0 the compiler is entitled to render a wipe either as a call or as inline zeroing. An extractor that knows only the call form reports the control as lost at -O1 and the measurement is then worthless.
ir.wipe-effect.discriminates: LOST from NOT_APPLICABLE. When the count falls to zero, the verdict is decided by whether a stack object of the size the effect acted on still exists in the unit at the post-optimisation checkpoint. If none does, the buffer was promoted out of memory and the question no longer has the same referent.
degradationRisk: Indirect calls are not counted: getCalledFunction returns null for them, so a wipe reached through a function pointer reads as absent. This biases towards a visible false positive rather than silence.

The promoted-object test matches by allocation size, and it is a CENSUS rather than an existence test: it compares how many objects of the size the effect acted on are allocated before and after. Two allocas of the same size in one unit therefore do not defeat it -- the count falls with the promoted one and the verdict is correctly NOT_APPLICABLE. What defeats it is a pass that CREATES an object of that size while the subject's is promoted, holding the count steady so that a buffer which left memory is reported LOST. Inlining does exactly that, which is why no source-level size discipline prevents it: measured 2026-08-17, a unit with one 192-byte buffer promoted away and a static helper's own 192-byte local inlined in reads LOST with its control still holding. Again a visible error rather than a silent one.
An alloca whose size is not statically known contributes no size, and the test degrades to 'no stack object survives in the unit at all'.
Anything unrecognised in the escape walk is treated as an escape, which pins the object and pushes the verdict towards LOST.

The symbol list is configuration. A project that wipes through its own helper, or builds with -fno-builtin-memset, changes what the effect is spelled as; a list that does not name it reads as ABSENT. The co-resident control is what catches this -- see the pc4 cell.
The zero-store half recognises stores of a zero constant. A wipe with a non-zero fill byte, or one lowered to a vectorised loop rather than to a store of a zero constant, is not counted by that half.
Cross-translation-unit inlining under LTO moves the effect into a different unit. The verdict becomes NOT_APPLICABLE and the property has to be re-scoped; it does not silently pass.

The zero-store half counts ANY store of a zero constant whose underlying object is an alloca in the unit or a pointer parameter of it. There is no requirement that the object be the one the property is about, no size floor, and no relation to the configured symbol list, so an ordinary zero-initialised local -- an `int flag = 0;`, or a loop counter -- is counted as the effect. This is the one risk in this list that errs towards PRESENT: measured 2026-08-17, a unit whose 181-byte wipe had been removed still read PRESENT with a held control because an unrelated zero-initialised local survived, and the same over-count lifts a one-wipe unit to a count of 2 at -O0 through a `for` loop's induction variable. Every other entry here errs towards a visible ABSENT or LOST; this one reports a defence that is not there.

ir.guarded-call.counts: Call sites to a configured deny or reject symbol, counted only while some conditional branch in the unit still tests a value. A branch on a constant decides nothing, so the call it leads to is waiting to be swept up rather than protecting anything.
ir.guarded-call.discriminates: LOST from NOT_APPLICABLE. For this class NOT_APPLICABLE has one cause -- the unit was inlined away -- because a branch has no memory object to be promoted out of.
degradationRisk: The live-branch test is per unit, not per call. Another live conditional branch elsewhere in the same function keeps an already-folded guard counted, which biases towards PRESENT. That is the dangerous direction, and it is why this extractor is marked implemented only for the single-guard shape its fixture has.
A guard expressed as a select, as arithmetic, or as a table lookup is not a branch and is not seen.
The guarded call must be to a resolvable named symbol; an indirect deny path is not counted.

A guard whose condition is folded by profile or by a build-time constant is reported as LOST, which is correct, but a guard the compiler merely moved into a caller is reported the same way unless the property is scoped to the caller.

ir.forbidden-callee.counts: Call sites to a configured forbidden symbol, resolved from the call instruction, inside one IR function. Opposite polarity to the other two: a non-zero count is the finding.
degradationRisk: IR is not the artefact. A forbidden call can arrive at link time, from a static library, from a relocation, or through inline asm, and none of that is visible at an IR checkpoint. Every must-not-appear property is therefore at most 'partial' here, and its authoritative checkpoint is object or linked.
Indirect calls are not counted, so a forbidden entry point reached through a table reads as absent.

The control for this polarity is a unit where the forbidden call is certainly still present -- that is what shows the extractor can still see one at this optimisation level. A control chosen the other way round proves nothing.

invocation.flag-set.counts: Tokens of the normalised command line, matched against policy.flags.required (VG-CFG-004), policy.flags.forbidden (VG-CFG-002) and policy.flags.optLevels (VG-CFG-003). Response files are expanded first, and a response file that cannot be read is exit 3 rather than a clean command line.
invocation.flag-set.whyItIsHere: This entry was missing while the component it describes was shipped and tested (compiler/driver/lib/flags.mjs, exercised by test/flags.test.mjs and test/driver-e2e.test.mjs). Its absence is why several must-be-configured entries below said `unimplemented` and why the write-up that reads this file would have reported a kind with no implementation at all. The catalogue is a tracked file: an omission here is an untrue statement about the tree it sits in.
invocation.flag-set.discriminates: A flag that is absent from the command line, from a flag that could not be read. The second is exit 3 and is never reported as the first.
degradationRisk: A flag present in one translation unit's command line and absent from another's is two invocations, and this extractor sees one at a time. Only the artefact shows what was actually linked, and the artefact half of this kind has no consumer.
Matching is against normalised tokens. A flag delivered through an environment variable the driver could not read makes the command line unreadable, which is exit 3 by design rather than a pass.
The optimisation level is read as written. A build system that rewrites -O2 into -O3 downstream of the recorded invocation is not visible here.

artifact.hardening-fields.counts: Structural fields of the finished image, not lines of a tool's output: e_type together with PT_INTERP for position independence, the PF_X bit of PT_GNU_STACK for a non-executable stack, and PT_GNU_RELRO together with DT_BIND_NOW / DF_BIND_NOW for relocation-readonly. The record names the field that decided each.
artifact.hardening-fields.whyItIsHere: The `artifact` checkpoint had no owner, so `policy.artifact.require` was a key the schema accepted and nothing read -- a policy the build ignores while appearing to honour it. This is the reader. It is the artefact half of must-be-configured: invocation.flag-set says what was asked for, this says what was got, and a build can pass the first and fail the second.
artifact.hardening-fields.discriminates: Full relocation-readonly from partial. Partial is the state a build regresses into, and a boolean reading reports it as a pass. Also NOT_APPLICABLE from PRESENT: a shared object has no PT_INTERP, and its position independence is a different question rather than a satisfied one.
degradationRisk: Four requirement names it accepts are not decided here at all -- stack-protector, fortify, no-debug-path and build-id. Each is exit 3 when a policy requires it, never a pass. Reporting an undecidable requirement as satisfied is the failure this refuses.
A static read cannot see protection a loader or a post-link tool changes at runtime.
The image must parse as ELF64 LSB. Anything else is exit 3 -- could not look -- and never exit 0.

artifact.section-flags.counts: Segments and sections whose flag bits carry write and execute at once, read from the flag words themselves.
artifact.section-flags.whyItIsHere: The one must-not-appear question in this catalogue that needs no control, because it is a structural field rather than a pattern match: there is no oracle here that can quietly stop matching. Recorded separately from artifact.hardening-fields because it answers a different kind -- what must not be there, rather than what must be configured -- and merging them would put one status on two questions.
artifact.section-flags.discriminates: A hit from a clean image, with both directions measured. A detector that has only ever fired has not been shown to stop firing.
degradationRisk: Only the linked image is read. A relocatable object carries the flags too, so a writable-executable section introduced and dropped before link is not seen.
Flag bits are what the image states. Runtime protection changes are outside a static read.

_notAnExtractor.artifactByteScan.whyThisIsNotListedAsAnExtractor: compiler/elf-verifier scans artefact bytes for forbidden sequences against required control sequences, and that machinery works -- a control string absent from the image makes the scan BROKEN at exit 3 rather than clean, which is the whole point of requiring controls. It is NOT registered as an extractor for notappear.test-credential, notappear.internal-url, unobservable.secret-literal or unobservable.stale-credential, and the reason is a gap in the FIXTURES rather than in the code. Every fixture in the matrix that carries the control string also carries the forbidden string, so the scanner has been shown to report a hit and to refuse a broken control, and has never once been shown to report CLEAN with a live control and a forbidden string configured. Until an image exists that holds the control and not the secret, the satisfied case is unmeasured, and a status column that said otherwise would be describing code rather than measurement. Measured 2026-08-16; the fixture generator is compiler/elf-verifier/artefact-fixtures.sh.

checkpointOwners._note: Written when this catalogue was the only thing in the directory, and every entry said nothing owned the checkpoint. Three of the five acquired an owner in the same batch, and a catalogue that still said otherwise was a tracked file asserting something untrue about the tree it is in. Corrected against the sources, not against a report of them.
checkpointOwners.ast: IntentGate (compiler/clang-plugin) classifies a lexical finding as Confirmed, Rejected or Refined and derives requirements from it. It does not yet record property STATE at this checkpoint, so no property below names ast as its observation point.
checkpointOwners.after-pass: PropertyObserver (compiler/pass-instrumentation/observer), which records (pass, IR unit) pairs and the whole state history.
checkpointOwners.object: Partially owned. compiler/elf-verifier reads objects and linked images for the INTRODUCTION question -- what appeared that no permitted origin explains. It does not yet answer the must-not-appear or must-remain-unobservable questions, which need a forbidden-string and secret-residue extractor that does not exist.
checkpointOwners.linked: compiler/elf-verifier, same scope and same limit as object.
checkpointOwners.invocation: compiler/driver normalises the command line, including the tokens behind -Xclang, -Wl, and a response file, and checks flags.required / flags.forbidden / flags.optLevels against the policy -- and the environment override that edits the line before clang sees it. That is the must-be-configured kind, at this checkpoint, implemented.
checkpointOwners.artifact: compiler/elf-verifier reads the finished binary structurally (Elf64_Ehdr / Elf64_Phdr / dynamic entries) rather than by parsing a tool's prose. Corrected 2026-08-16: this said policy.artifact.require has no consumer, and it now has one -- lib/artifact-policy.mjs decides PIE, NX, full RELRO and writable-executable sections, and artefact-require.mjs is its command line. Four of the names a policy may use are still not decided here (stack-protector, fortify, no-debug-path, build-id) and each is exit 3 when required rather than a pass, so the checkpoint is owned but not completely.

kindCoverage.must-survive: partial -- two extractors, both measured, both at IR checkpoints only
kindCoverage.must-not-appear: partial -- one extractor at IR checkpoints, and one structural extractor at the linked image for the writable-executable question, measured in both directions on 2026-08-16. The string-shaped entries in this kind are still unimplemented, and the obstacle is the fixture matrix rather than the scanner: every image in it that carries the control string also carries the forbidden one, so a clean scan under a live control has never been observed. See _notAnExtractor.artifactByteScan
kindCoverage.must-originate-from: partial -- compiler/elf-verifier classifies symbols, sections and initialisers into source-derived / generator-derived / dependency-derived / toolchain-derived / linker-generated / runtime-support, with a toolchain baseline keyed on (toolchain digest, flag set, link form) and six negative controls at Unexplained = 0. No property below is yet declared against it in this catalogue
kindCoverage.must-be-configured: partial -- compiler/driver checks required, forbidden and optimisation-level flags at the invocation checkpoint, and refuses to call a command line clean when an environment override made it unreadable. Corrected 2026-08-16: the artefact half is no longer absent. PIE, NX and RELRO are read from the finished image, with the partial-RELRO case measured rather than collapsed into a boolean, so this kind now has both what was asked for and what was got. Stack protector and FORTIFY remain undecided here and are exit 3 when a policy requires them
kindCoverage.must-remain-unobservable: none -- no extractor, no checkpoint, no measurement

properties.title: A buffer holding a secret is cleared before it goes out of scope

oracle.detail: Call sites to the wipe symbol, resolved from the call instruction, plus inline zero stores into the object. Never a symbol-table lookup: a deleted call leaves its declaration behind, and a name lookup goes on answering 'present' until an unrelated pass sweeps it.
oracle.controlRule: A co-resident unit whose wipe is observable and therefore not removable. A run in which the control's count also reached zero is a broken measurement, not a finding.

degradationRisk: See ir.wipe-effect. The one specific to this property: the checkpoints stop at the end of the IR optimiser, so a wipe that survives to post-opt IR and is then dropped by instruction selection is reported PRESENT here. That is measured -- at -O1 this fixture's wipe survives every IR checkpoint and the prototype workspace attributes its loss to the backend -- and it is a scope limit, not a disagreement.
NOT_APPLICABLE is not a pass. The record marks it completesTheCheck: false so a caller maps it to exit 3.

properties.title: A deny path stays reachable behind a condition the compiler cannot decide

oracle.counts: call sites, gated on a live conditional branch
oracle.detail: Call sites to the deny symbol, counted only while some conditional branch in the unit still tests a value.
oracle.controlRule: A co-resident unit whose condition comes from outside the translation unit, so that neither the branch nor the deny call can be folded away.

degradationRisk: See ir.guarded-call. The per-unit live-branch test is the weak point and it fails towards PRESENT.

A guard removed because the build genuinely decided it at compile time and a guard removed by mistake look identical here. That is the correct reading -- both are the property not being enforced at run time -- but it means a build with a legitimately constant policy will report LOST and needs a scope or a policy entry, not a code change.

properties.title: An authorisation decision is still taken at run time

oracle.counts: call sites, gated on a live conditional branch
oracle.detail: Same extractor and same rule as survive.fail-closed-branch, configured with the deny symbol of the authorisation path. It is listed separately because a policy names one or the other and the scopes differ.
oracle.controlRule: As survive.fail-closed-branch.

degradationRisk: See ir.guarded-call.
An authorisation check whose result is consumed rather than branched on -- returned to a caller, stored in a flag -- is not a guarded call and is not seen by this extractor at all.

properties.title: A bounds check reaches its trap
properties.statusDetail: ir.guarded-call takes llvm.trap and the __ubsan_handle_* family as effect symbols and would count the trap edges. Nothing in this repository has measured it, so no cell may be quoted as evidence for it.

oracle.counts: call sites, gated on a live conditional branch
oracle.detail: Trap call sites reached from a conditional branch that still tests a value.
oracle.controlRule: A co-resident check on a length the compiler cannot know.

degradationRisk: A bounds check the compiler proved redundant is removed legitimately, and this extractor cannot tell that from a check removed because the bound became a constant for the wrong reason. Without a fixture that separates the two, a LOST here means 'look at this', not 'this is a defect'.
See ir.guarded-call.

properties.title: A validation routine still runs on the path that needs it
properties.statusDetail: Needs an extractor for 'this call site must remain on this path', which is neither the wipe shape nor the guarded-branch shape. None is written.

oracle.detail: Would count call sites to the validator that dominate the use of the validated value. Reachability, not presence, is the question, and nothing here answers it.
oracle.controlRule: Undecided -- a control for a dominance property is not the same shape as a control for a count.

degradationRisk: Not applicable: there is no extractor to degrade.

properties.title: An audit record is still emitted for the event
properties.statusDetail: A plain 'this call must survive' extractor -- ir.wipe-effect without its zero-store half and without its memory-object discriminator -- is not written. Configuring ir.wipe-effect for it would report a promoted-object NOT_APPLICABLE for a property that has no buffer, which is a wrong answer rather than a missing one.

oracle.detail: Would count call sites to the audit symbol inside the unit.
oracle.controlRule: A co-resident audit call the compiler cannot remove.

degradationRisk: Not applicable: there is no extractor to degrade.

properties.title: A call to a symbol the policy forbids
properties.statusDetail: Measured at the IR checkpoints. The checkpoints that decide this kind -- object and linked -- have no implementation, so an IR-only clean reading is not an answer and must not be reported as one.

oracle.detail: Call sites to the forbidden symbol, resolved from the call instruction, inside one IR function. A non-zero count is the finding.
oracle.controlRule: Inverted for this polarity: the control is a co-resident unit where the forbidden call is certainly still present, which is what shows the extractor can still see one at this optimisation level.

degradationRisk: See ir.forbidden-callee. The decisive one: the call can arrive after this checkpoint, from a library or from the linker, and nothing here would see it.

properties.title: A debug or diagnostic entry point in a release build
properties.statusDetail: The extractor takes the configuration. Nothing here has measured it, and an endpoint that is a defined symbol rather than a call site is not what this extractor counts.

oracle.counts: call sites at IR; would be defined and exported symbols at object
oracle.detail: The two are different questions. An endpoint nobody calls is still an endpoint, so the call-site count is the wrong oracle for this property and the object-level symbol table is the right one.
oracle.unitOfCount: one IR function at IR; the symbol table at object
oracle.controlRule: A co-resident endpoint that is expected to be present.

degradationRisk: Counting call sites for a property about reachable entry points is a category error that happens to be cheap. Marked candidate rather than implemented for exactly that reason.

properties.title: A credential used by tests survives into a shipped artefact
properties.statusDetail: A byte-sequence question about an object file. There is no IR reading of it that is not a guess, and nothing in compiler/ reads objects.

oracle.detail: Would compare extracted byte sequences against policy.artifact.forbidStrings and report VG-ART-005.
oracle.unitOfCount: the object, then the linked image
oracle.controlRule: A string that is expected to be present, so that an extractor which has stopped finding anything is distinguishable from an artefact that is clean.

degradationRisk: Not applicable: there is no extractor to degrade.

properties.title: An internal hostname or URL in a shipped artefact

oracle.detail: As notappear.test-credential.
oracle.unitOfCount: the object, then the linked image
oracle.controlRule: As notappear.test-credential.

degradationRisk: Not applicable: there is no extractor to degrade.

properties.title: A section that is both writable and executable
properties.statusDetail: Promoted 2026-08-16. The artefact verifier this entry said did not exist now does: compiler/elf-verifier/lib/artifact-policy.mjs reads the flag bits and artefact-require.mjs is its command line. Both polarities were measured on this machine against the fixture matrix, which is what `implemented` means in this file -- the wx-on image reports one hit and the VG-ART-004 finding at exit 2, and the hardened image reports zero at exit 0. A promotion on the strength of the code alone would be the error this file made before 2026-08-10 and corrected.

oracle.detail: Reads the section and segment flags and decides from the flag bits, never from a tool's human-readable line, and records which field decided it.
oracle.controlRule: None: a structural flag has no oracle that can quietly stop working the way a pattern match can.

degradationRisk: The object checkpoint is still unimplemented. A relocatable object can carry the flags too, and only the linked image is read here, so a W+X section introduced and then dropped before link is invisible to this entry.
The decision is the flag bits as the image states them. A loader or a post-link tool that changes protection at runtime is outside what a static read can see, and this entry does not claim otherwise.

The two granularities are not equally evidenced -- see evidence.granularity. The segment reading has never been produced by a real toolchain here, only by a byte writer, so a regression in it would not be caught by the fixture matrix.

evidence.readings: wx-on: one hit, finding VG-ART-004, exit 2. hardened: zero, exit 0. The negative is recorded beside the positive because a detector that has only ever fired has not been shown to stop.
evidence.granularity: The wx-on hit is a SECTION (.vgwx, sh_flags = ALLOC|WRITE|EXECINSTR), not a segment: this was checked by reading the hit rather than assumed from the fixture's name. No row of the matrix carries a PT_LOAD with PF_W|PF_X, because objcopy re-flags the section after the link and the containing PT_LOAD stays RW-. The segment half of this extractor is therefore evidenced only by a synthetic image assembled byte by byte in test/synth-elf64.mjs, which shows the decider reads the field it says it reads and shows nothing about whether a toolchain emits it. Recorded because `implemented` on the strength of the fixture name would have been an over-claim about the half a real link never produced.

properties.title: Cryptographic code comes from the approved implementation
properties.statusDetail: Corrected 2026-08-10. This said the whole kind has no implementation and that nothing here classifies where a definition came from; compiler/elf-verifier/classify.mjs does exactly that, sorting symbols, sections and initialisers into the six permitted origins against a toolchain baseline, and this file's own kindCoverage says so. The entry stays `unimplemented` because the QUESTION differs, not because the component is missing: the classifier answers introduction — what appeared that no permitted origin explains — while this property asks attribution, whether a definition came from the APPROVED implementation, and nothing compares an origin against policy.link.allowedObjects yet. That distinction is the reason to keep the status, and stating it is the reason not to keep the old sentence.

oracle.detail: Would attribute each definition in the linked image to the object or archive member that provided it, and compare that against policy.link.allowedObjects and allowedLibraries.
oracle.unitOfCount: one symbol definition in the linked image
oracle.controlRule: A symbol whose origin is known and expected, so that an attribution step that has stopped resolving anything is visible.

degradationRisk: Not applicable: there is no extractor to degrade.

properties.title: Generated code came from the recorded generator and input

oracle.detail: As origin.crypto-implementation, with the generator's output as the permitted origin.
oracle.unitOfCount: one symbol definition in the linked image
oracle.controlRule: As origin.crypto-implementation.

degradationRisk: Not applicable: there is no extractor to degrade.

properties.title: An external library is the one the policy pinned

oracle.detail: Would compare the digest of each library actually opened by the link against the pin. A name match alone is not enough -- a file with the right name and different bytes is a different library.
oracle.controlRule: A pinned input whose digest is expected to match, so that a digest step returning nothing is distinguishable from a clean link.

degradationRisk: Not applicable: there is no extractor to degrade.

properties.title: The build ran at an optimisation level the policy has been evaluated at
properties.statusDetail: Corrected 2026-08-10. This entry said `unimplemented`, on the grounds that 'nothing here reads a command line'. That was true when it was written and false when it was read: compiler/driver/lib/flags.mjs compares the normalised command line against policy.flags.optLevels and reports VG-CFG-003, measured by test/flags.test.mjs and by test/driver-e2e.test.mjs. This same file's kindCoverage already said `partial` for the kind, so the catalogue contradicted itself, and anything generated from the per-property entries reported a shipped check as absent. IrCheckpoints still observes only the CONSEQUENCES of an optimisation level and never the flag; that remains a different claim and is still not a substitute.

oracle.detail: Compares the normalised command line against policy.flags.optLevels and reports VG-CFG-003. A property observed to survive -O1 has not been observed to survive -O3.
oracle.controlRule: None: a flag either is or is not in the argument vector.

degradationRisk: The level is read as written. A build system that rewrites the flag downstream of the recorded invocation is not visible at this checkpoint.
One invocation at a time. A project compiled at two levels has two records, and nothing here merges them.

properties.title: NDEBUG is set or unset as the policy requires
properties.statusDetail: Named here because it is the case this directory exists for: a security decision inside an assert disappears under NDEBUG, which is exactly the class of disappearance being detected. The shipped analyser flags that pattern at the source. Corrected 2026-08-10: this entry also said nothing here checks the FLAG, which stopped being true when the driver landed — -DNDEBUG is matched by policy.flags.required (VG-CFG-004) or policy.flags.forbidden (VG-CFG-002) like any other token, and an unreadable command line is exit 3 rather than a pass. What is still absent is an artefact-side confirmation that the define survived into what was built.

oracle.detail: Would look for -DNDEBUG in the normalised command line and report VG-CFG-002 or VG-CFG-001 depending on which list it is on.
oracle.controlRule: None.

degradationRisk: Corrected 2026-08-18. This array said 'Not applicable: there is no extractor to degrade.', which was left behind by the 2026-08-10 promotion recorded in statusDetail above: the entry became 'implemented' with invocation.flag-set named as its extractor, and the sentence saying no extractor exists was not removed. Inside one entry, three fields disagreed -- status said implemented, extractor named one, and this array said there was none to degrade. It is outside the calibration battery's fence (claims/degradation-claims.json fences only ir.wipe-effect, ir.guarded-call and ir.forbidden-callee, and names invocation.flag-set among the entries it does not cover), so correcting it moves no calibrated reading.

The real degradation is that the reading is of the COMMAND LINE and not of the artefact, so it degrades towards saying nothing rather than towards saying something false: a spelling the normaliser cannot resolve -- NDEBUG mentioned inside a -Wp, or -Xpreprocessor passthrough, or reached through a response file -- sets the axis to null (cmdline.mjs:400, 'ndebug: ndebugOpaque ? null : ndebug'), and a null axis is not matched on rather than defaulted to false. A build that defines NDEBUG through a form this reader cannot see is therefore UNREADABLE, never 'NDEBUG absent'.

What remains genuinely absent is the other half, and it is the half that would make this a property of the shipped binary: nothing confirms the define survived preprocessing into what was built. An assert compiled out under NDEBUG leaves no artefact-side trace for the flag-set extractor to find, which is why statusDetail calls the artefact-side confirmation still missing.
properties.evidence: compiler/driver/test/cmdline.test.mjs -- 'NDEBUG is tracked through -D and -U in argv order, in both spellings' (both -DNDEBUG and -D NDEBUG; -DNDEBUG=0 still counts as defined because assert.h asks only whether it is defined; -UNDEBUG later in argv order wins). Filled in 2026-08-18: this field read null while status read 'implemented', which the vocabulary at the top of this file defines as requiring a fixture in this repository that measures the property. The fixture existed; the field naming it did not, so the entry could not be checked against its own definition without going to look for one.

properties.title: The required sanitizers are enabled, and the forbidden ones are not

oracle.counts: normalised command-line flags, then runtime dependencies of the artefact
oracle.detail: The two disagree usefully: a flag can be present in one translation unit's command line and absent from another's, and only the artefact shows what was actually linked.
oracle.unitOfCount: one compiler invocation, then the linked image
oracle.controlRule: None.

degradationRisk: Not applicable: there is no extractor to degrade.

properties.title: Stack protection is on

oracle.counts: normalised command-line flags, then a structural field of the artefact
oracle.detail: Would be decided at the artefact from the presence of the guard references, never from a tool's summary line, and the record would say which field decided it.
oracle.unitOfCount: one compiler invocation, then the linked image
oracle.controlRule: None.

degradationRisk: Not applicable: there is no extractor to degrade.

properties.title: The image is position independent, non-executable where it should be, and fully read-only after relocation
properties.statusDetail: Promoted 2026-08-16, and it is the artefact half this kind was missing: `configured.optimisation-level` and `configured.ndebug` read the command line, which says what was ASKED for, while this reads the finished image, which says what was GOT. All three of PIE, NX and RELRO were measured in both directions on this machine, including the partial-RELRO case, which is the one a boolean reading would silently pass.

oracle.detail: The image type, the segment flags, and the presence of the relocation-readonly segment. Each is a field, not a line of output, and the record names the field.
oracle.controlRule: None.

degradationRisk: A shared object has no PT_INTERP and its position independence is not the same question as an executable's. The reading is NOT_APPLICABLE there rather than PRESENT, and a caller that treats NOT_APPLICABLE as a pass is reading it wrong.
RELRO has three readings and only one of them is full. A consumer that maps this to a boolean turns the partial case -- the one a build actually regresses into -- into a pass.

Four of the requirement names this component accepts are not decided by it at all: stack-protector, fortify, no-debug-path and build-id are exit 3 when required, never a pass. They are named here so the absence is in the catalogue rather than only in the source.

evidence.readings: pie-on/pie-off gave PRESENT/ABSENT, nx-on/nx-off gave PRESENT/ABSENT, and relro-full/part/none gave full/partial/none. Every negative exited 2 with a finding; every positive exited 0.

properties.title: Link-time optimisation, the target, and the linker are what the policy pinned
properties.statusDetail: Called out separately because LTO changes what every must-survive property means: it moves effects across translation units, so a property scoped to a unit can become NOT_APPLICABLE for reasons the policy author did not anticipate.

oracle.counts: normalised command-line flags and toolchain digests
oracle.detail: Would compare against policy.toolchain and policy.link.allowedLinkers, and fail closed on a digest that does not match the pin.
oracle.controlRule: None.

properties.title: A secret does not survive in the artefact or in memory after use
properties.statusDetail: This whole kind has no implementation in compiler/. The IR half of the story is covered by survive.secure-wipe, but 'the wipe is still in the IR' and 'the secret is not observable' are different claims, and this file does not let the first stand in for the second.

oracle.detail: Would look for the secret's bytes in the artefact, and separately for a wipe that reaches the storage at run time. A LOST on survive.secure-wipe is a sufficient reason to consider this property unmet; a PRESENT there is not sufficient to consider it met.
oracle.unitOfCount: the object, then the linked image
oracle.controlRule: A byte sequence expected to be present, so an extractor that has stopped finding anything is visible.

interfaceExtensionsRequested.note: compiler/schema/interfaces.md fixes six OBS_* names. IrCheckpoints needed five more and did not add them to that file, because the file says a component that needs a shape not listed there reports it rather than editing it. These are the names in use.

names.OBS_EXTRACTOR: which targeted extractor to run: ir.wipe-effect, ir.guarded-call or ir.forbidden-callee
names.OBS_PROPERTY_ID: the property id from this file that the run is about
names.OBS_FIXTURE_REL: the source path relative to the fixture root, so that no absolute path reaches a record
names.OBS_DISABLE_MEMOBJ_DISCRIMINATOR: positive control only: switches off the LOST/NOT_APPLICABLE discriminator so that a cell which should read NOT_APPLICABLE can be shown to read LOST without it
